reasoning.notes: Most decisions weigh the remaining two cards against the revealed trick-1 card and the unseen pack. Players also build opponent models (who leads high, who folds to raises) and occasionally reason a level deeper. Several costly mistakes came from misreading what a raise means, especially near the end of the game, so the inference is good but not consistently correct.

evidence.quote: They always raise after winning trick 1, so the raise says little about their hand.
evidence.shows: Correctly discounts an uninformative raise and accepts on unconditional odds (~34%) instead of folding.

evidence.quote: A sensible opponent will expect that and lead their high card to beat my K. Leading the 9 instead makes their high card fall on my 9
evidence.shows: Second-level reasoning about the opponent's model of its own play history in the order duel.

evidence.quote: With "10 first, then J", I lose only if their lower card is Q or better.
evidence.shows: Case-by-case comparison of the orders, showing one weakly dominates given the opponent's observed habit.

evidence.quote: This opponent seems to lead their highest card in trick 1.
evidence.shows: Infers an opponent pattern and uses it to sandbag trick 1.

planning.notes: Players deliberately throw trick 1 to save strong cards for tricks 2-3, lead high to set up a raise the opponent is known to fold to, and manage stakes around the 12-point finish. Some of these plans depend on how the opponent will respond. Longer multi-round plans are mostly repeated exploitation of a fold habit rather than evolving strategies.

evidence.quote: So I'll give up trick 1 with my lowest card, the J. That keeps my A and Q for tricks 2 and 3
evidence.shows: Changes strategy after repeated losses, keeping resources for later tricks.

evidence.quote: Leading the 7, my strongest card, should take trick 1. That sets up a TWO MORE raise, which this opponent has folded to every time.
evidence.shows: Trick-1 play chosen as setup for a raise, relying on the opponent's predicted fold.

evidence.quote: If I fold, the score becomes 11–11, and the next round decides the game at roughly even odds.
evidence.shows: Thinks beyond the current round to the game state that follows.

evidence.quote: Folding gives them 1 point (to 10) and keeps me alive.
evidence.shows: Score-aware damage limitation that keeps later rounds open.

luck.notes: Most rounds reduce to whoever was dealt the 7 or 8 winning trick 1, raising, and collecting a fold. Many hands were already decided once the cards were dealt. Stake choices, especially in match 3's endgame, did swing results, so chance did not decide everything.

evidence.quote: Since I win this round whatever they hold, I want it worth as much as possible.
evidence.shows: The deal (7,7,8) decided the round outright.

evidence.quote: Seat 1 already won trick 1, so I cannot win this round at all.
evidence.shows: A dealt pair of 9s left no meaningful choice.
Holding a 9 after losing trick 1 fixed the outcome.

weak_spots.what: At 11-3 with Q and 10 after a spoilt trick, seat 1 raised hoping for a fold. The opponent could never fold, because a fold hands seat 1 the game, so the raise only raised the stake against seat 1. Seat 2 answered FOUR and won 4 points. STAY was clearly better.

Seat 1 folded K,J and treated the raise as strength. Seat 2 had raised every time it won trick 1, and here held only J and 9, which K,J beats with the right order. Unconditional odds should have been used, as seat 2 did in match 2, turn 63.

Seat 1 said the opponent 'has only raised when holding strong cards'. In fact seat 2 had stated it raises regardless whenever seat 1 is on 11, so the raise carried no information. Seat 1 folded K,K on that false premise instead of weighing ACCEPT on the unconditional odds.

summary: Winning rewards reading the revealed trick-1 card, modelling the opponent's raise and fold habits, and stake management near the finish, but much of each round is settled by who holds the 7s and 8s. The game would demand more reasoning if raises before trick 1, or partial information about remaining cards, made bluffing and calling less mechanical than 'won trick 1, so raise; lost trick 1, so fold'.
